analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to negotiate Medicare drug prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on the first day of the 114th Congress and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate drug prices for Medicare's Part D prescription drug benefit directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, replacing the 2003 rule that the government stay out of those negotiations. It would have required the Secretary to report to Congress twice a year on the prices and discounts achieved. Beneficiaries and taxpayers stood to pay less for drugs; brand-name drug makers stood to receive lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million people enrolled in Medicare Part D drug plans, through lower drug prices and premiums, and taxpayers, who help fund the program. Private plan sponsors could also seek deeper discounts below the government-negotiated price.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate the prices, discounts, rebates, and other concessions that drug manufacturers may charge to Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations [S2][S3].
Strikes the 2003 'noninterference' provision, which barred the government from interfering in negotiations between drug makers and private plans [S3].
Plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage plans may still obtain discounts below the government-negotiated price, and the bill preserves existing formulary rules and beneficiary access protections [S3].
Requires the Secretary to report to the relevant congressional committees every six months on the negotiations conducted and the prices and discounts achieved, starting June 1, 2016 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would receive lower Medicare-negotiated prices for Part D drugs and lose revenue they earn under the current non-negotiation system.

drawbacks.text: A single government negotiator might not achieve savings much larger than what private Part D plans already win through pharmacy benefit managers, a reason critics long cited against direct negotiation; the bill's own text acknowledges plans already negotiate discounts by preserving their ability to go below the negotiated price [S3].

Capping Medicare's payments to drug makers at negotiated prices would reduce revenue for brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, a cost that critics argue could affect future investment in new medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: lower drug prices for tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, paid for out of the revenue of brand-name drug makers. The bill was modest in design — it preserved private plans' ability to negotiate further discounts and imposed no formulary mandates — so its main uncertainty is whether one federal negotiator would extract larger savings than private plans already do. It never got far enough for that question to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 6, 2015, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled a vote or markup, so the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) introduced the bill on January 6, 2015, with five original cosponsors: Sens. Sanders, Shaheen, Kaine, King, and Blumenthal [S3].
The bill was read twice on the day of introduction and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; the action history shows no further action for the remainder of the 114th Congress [S5].

The bill would have replaced the statutory 'noninterference' provision in Medicare Part D, which bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating drug prices on behalf of beneficiaries [S3].
The bill's final cosponsor list totaled nine senators: seven Democrats and two Independents; no Republicans signed on [S4].
Because the Congress ended on January 3, 2017, the bill received no vote in either chamber and made no law [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: they kept the existing Medicare Part D system, in which federal law bars the government from negotiating their prices, at no cost to themselves. Medicare beneficiaries continued paying the negotiated-elsewhere prices the bill was written to lower.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 114th Congress and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 9 Senate cosponsors (7 Democrats, 2 Independents)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Sanders, Shaheen, Kaine, King, and Blumenthal.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the committee's action history shows no action for the life of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry with a direct financial stake in Medicare drug pricing
against.what_they_did: Has long campaigned against letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices, preserving the noninterference rule the bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill was referred to a Republican-chaired committee that took no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would require the government to negotiate Medicare prices, reducing what these companies can charge on tens of millions of prescriptions. Their gain under the status quo comes directly from what beneficiaries and taxpayers pay.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Negotiated prices would lower their input costs, but the bill preserves their ability to seek deeper discounts below the negotiated price and keeps existing formulary and access rules in place. Lower drug costs flow through to lower premiums for beneficiaries.

Government negotiation would take over part of the price-setting work these intermediaries perform for Part D plans, but the bill lets plans keep negotiating discounts below the government price, leaving them a continued role.
